title: Domino's Menu with Prices (2026): The Complete USA Guide
excerpt: A real, no-nonsense look at the Domino's menu and what it costs in 2026 — pizzas, sides, chicken, desserts and the deals that quietly cut your bill.
author: editorial-team

faqs.question: How much is a large pizza at Domino's in 2026?
faqs.answer: A Large (14") cheese pizza is typically around $11.99 and a Large pepperoni around $12.99 at carryout, though prices vary by location. Ordering through Mix & Match or the $6.99 Each deal is usually cheaper. Verify at official checkout.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest way to order Domino's?
faqs.answer: Carryout deals and the $6.99 Each promotion are consistently the cheapest routes. Mix & Match lets you combine two or more items at a fixed per-item price, and Domino's Rewards earns you a free pizza over time.

faqs.question: Are Domino's prices the same at every location?
faqs.answer: No. Domino's stores are individually franchised and set their own prices, so the same pizza can cost different amounts in different cities. Always confirm the final total at checkout.

faqs.question: Does Domino's still have the Mix & Match deal?
faqs.answer: Mix & Match has been Domino's flagship value deal for years and remains widely available. The exact per-item price changes periodically, so check the current offer on the official app.

faqs.question: How much is a medium 2-topping pizza at Domino's?
faqs.answer: A Medium (12") two-topping pizza is typically around $11.49 at menu price, but it's usually cheaper as the classic Mix & Match item. It's one of the most deal-friendly orders on the menu.

faqs.question: What is the most expensive item on the Domino's menu?
faqs.answer: The loaded specialty pizzas in Large size sit at the top, usually around $16.99–$17.99 at menu price. Even those drop to the per-item deal rate through Mix & Match, so you rarely need to pay full price.

faqs.question: Does Domino's have a cheap lunch option?
faqs.answer: Yes. Hot sandwiches around $6.99–$7.99, oven-baked pasta near $7.99, and boneless chicken from $8.99 all make solid single-person lunches, especially through a value deal.

faqs.question: How often do Domino's prices change?
faqs.answer: Core menu prices are fairly stable, but individual franchises adjust them and deals rotate regularly. We refresh these example prices monthly and always tell you to verify the live total at checkout.

content:
So, What Does Domino's Actually Cost in 2026?

Let's be honest about something first. There's no single, magic price list for Domino's, no matter how much we all wish there were. Every store is its own little business, franchised and priced by whoever runs it. That corner shop near you and the one three towns over can charge different amounts for the exact same Large pepperoni. Wild, right? It catches people off guard all the time — they see a price online, drive over, and the total's a couple dollars off from what they expected.

So treat every number on this page as a solid ballpark rather than gospel. I've built these figures from what stores commonly post, and I keep them current month to month. When it's time to actually pay, though, the checkout screen is the only price that counts. Fair enough? Good. Now let's walk the whole menu, category by category, with real example prices for each — and I'll flag where the value hides and where people quietly overspend without noticing.

Pizza: Where Most People Start

A build-your-own pizza gets priced two ways at once — the size you pick, and how many toppings you pile on. A Large cheese usually lands around $11.99, and each extra topping tacks on a buck-fifty to two-fifty or so. Nothing dramatic on its own, but it adds up fast if you go wild. I've watched people turn a twelve-dollar pizza into a twenty-dollar one just by saying yes to every topping the app cheerfully suggests.

PizzaSmall (10")Medium (12")Large (14")
Cheese~$7.99~$9.99~$11.99
Pepperoni~$8.99~$10.99~$12.99
2-topping build~$9.49~$11.49~$13.49

Here's the part people forget: crust choice doesn't just change the taste, it changes the mood of the whole meal. Hand Tossed is the safe, pillowy default that pleases almost everyone. Handmade Pan is the indulgent one, buttery and thick, and it's the crust I reach for when I want pizza to feel like a treat. Crunchy Thin is for folks who think most pizza has too much bread — light, crisp, and it lets the toppings do the talking. Brooklyn Style goes big and foldable. And there's a Gluten Free option in a small size if wheat's off the table. For how the sizes stack up on value, the pizza sizes guide breaks it all down.

How Toppings Change the Math

Toppings are where two identical-looking orders end up costing wildly different amounts. A plain cheese and a five-topping monster are the same base pizza, just priced worlds apart. My honest advice? Pick two or three toppings you genuinely love rather than six you're lukewarm on. It tastes better and costs less — a rare combination. And if you're going heavy on toppings anyway, jump to a specialty pizza, because you'll usually pay less for the same load. More on that right now.

Specialty Pizzas Are Sneaky Good Value

Now here's the thing about the specialty pies. They come pre-loaded, so the sticker price looks higher — a Large usually sits between $15.99 and $17.99. That number scares people off. But here's what they miss: almost all of them qualify for Mix & Match. That means you can grab a fully loaded ExtravaganZZa or a Philly Cheese Steak for the same per-item price as a plain two-topping. Read that again. More toppings, same money. Ordering a specialty inside a deal is one of the easiest wins on the whole menu, and it's the move I make nine times out of ten.

Specialty PizzaLarge ExampleBest For
ExtravaganZZa~$16.99Meat lovers, big appetites
Philly Cheese Steak~$16.99No-pork, cheesesteak fans
Pacific Veggie~$16.99Vegetarians
MeatZZa~$16.99All-meat cravings

Which specialty should you pick? If you love meat, the MeatZZa and ExtravaganZZa are your lane. Vegetarian? The Pacific Veggie is genuinely good and doesn't feel like a compromise. Want something that breaks the tomato-sauce mold entirely? The Philly Cheese Steak skips red sauce for a cheese base and tastes more like a sandwich than a pizza — in the best possible way.

Pasta, Chicken and Sandwiches

People sleep on the non-pizza menu, and I get why — you go to Domino's for pizza. But they're missing out. Oven-baked pasta like Chicken Alfredo or Italian Sausage Marinara runs roughly $7.99 to $8.99 and travels surprisingly well. Boneless chicken and wings start near $8.99 and make a great add-on when a pizza alone won't quite cut it. And the hot sandwiches — the Italian, the Chicken Bacon Ranch — hover around $6.99 to $7.99 and are quietly one of the better lunch options nobody talks about. Our Domino's sides menu guide prices up the whole non-pizza lineup, tots and desserts included.

Wings8 pieces~$9.49
Hot sandwichesEach~$6.99–$7.99

Sides, Sweets and Something to Drink

The sides are where the real bargains hide, and honestly where I do most of my damage. Stuffed Cheesy Bread, Parmesan Bread Bites, Garlic Bread Twists — most sit in the $6.99 to $7.99 range and drop even lower inside a deal. Stuffed Cheesy Bread in particular is the one I'd tell a first-timer to try before anything else. For dessert? The Chocolate Lava Crunch Cakes are the move, around $4.99, molten in the middle, and genuinely worth it. The Marbled Cookie Brownie is the shareable pick if there's a crowd. Round it out with a 2-liter of Coke and you've fed the whole table for less than you'd think.

The Golden Rule: Don't Pay Full Price

If you take one thing from this entire guide, take this. You should almost never pay menu price at Domino's. The Mix & Match deal and the $6.99 Each promo exist precisely so you don't have to. Build your order inside one of them from the very first click. Then add Domino's Rewards on top, because every qualifying order earns points toward a free pizza whether you use a deal or not. And if you can swing by and grab it yourself, carryout beats delivery every single time once the fee and tip land. The full step-by-step is in my money-saving guide, and browsing the live coupons page before you order takes ten seconds and pays for itself.

The Mistake I See Constantly

Want to know the most common way people overpay? They add items one at a time at full price instead of building the order around a deal, then wonder why the total quietly crept past thirty bucks. Two minutes of planning — deal first, carryout if you can, signed into rewards — routinely knocks a quarter to nearly half off the total. It's not a secret hack. It's just paying attention, which most of us don't do when we're hungry and rushing.

How to Build a Smart Full Order

Let me put it all together with a real example. Say you're feeding a family of four. Two large pizzas through Mix & Match, one order of Stuffed Cheesy Bread, and a 2-liter. Order it carryout, signed into rewards. That's a complete dinner with leftovers, at a price that doesn't sting, plus points banking toward your next free pizza. That's the whole game — deal, side, drink, carryout, rewards. Repeat it and you'll consistently pay less than the person next to you ordering the same food at full price.

One Honest Caveat

I check these prices against posted menus and refresh this page monthly, but Domino's can change a price or pull a deal whenever it feels like it. Nothing here is a promise. This is an independent, unofficial guide written by people who just really like ordering pizza well and can't stand watching folks overpay for it. For live prices, current deals, and to actually place your order, the official Domino's app is your friend. Use this page to plan smart, then let checkout confirm the details. That's the deal — you plan, they cook, everybody wins.

title: Domino's Coupons & Promo Codes (2026): Every Deal Explained
excerpt: Skip the coupon-hunting rabbit hole. Here's how Domino's deals really work in 2026, which ones are worth it, and how to squeeze them together.
author: priya-nair

faqs.question: Where do I enter a Domino's promo code?
faqs.answer: On the official Domino's app or website, promo codes are entered in the coupon or deals section at checkout. Many deals apply automatically when you add qualifying items to your cart.

faqs.question: Does Domino's have a coupon for a free pizza?
faqs.answer: The most reliable way to get a free pizza is through Domino's Rewards, which awards a free medium two-topping pizza once you accumulate enough points. Occasional promotions also offer free items with a qualifying purchase.

faqs.question: Are Domino's online coupons better than in-store?
faqs.answer: Online and app-based deals are usually the best, since digital pricing tends to reflect the current national promotions. Carryout deals in particular are often exclusive to online ordering.

faqs.question: How do I get the cheapest Domino's order?
faqs.answer: Build your order inside Mix & Match or $6.99 Each, choose carryout to skip the delivery fee, order in the app, and stay signed into Domino's Rewards. Stacking those four routinely cuts 25–40% off.

faqs.question: Can I use more than one coupon at a time?
faqs.answer: Generally no — you can't stack two coupons on the same items. But you can combine a value deal with carryout and rewards, which saves you three different ways without needing two codes.

faqs.question: Do Domino's coupon codes expire?
faqs.answer: Yes, limited-time codes expire and the standing deals rotate. Always confirm the offer is live in the official app before you rely on it.

faqs.question: Are these coupon codes guaranteed to work?
faqs.answer: No. The offers here are examples for guidance, not guaranteed codes. Verify the live deal on the official Domino's app, and never trust a third party promising a guaranteed free-pizza code.

content:
Stop Hunting for Random Codes

Here's a confession from someone who's spent way too many hours on this stuff: most of the Domino's promo codes floating around the internet are junk. Expired, fake, or region-locked to somewhere that isn't where you live. You paste them in, hit apply, and get that little red error message that quietly ruins your evening. The truth is, Domino's doesn't really run on secret codes. It runs on a handful of recurring deals, and once you understand those, you'll never need to Google a coupon again. Promise.

So instead of sending you on a scavenger hunt across a dozen sketchy coupon sites, let me walk you through the deals that actually matter — what each one does, who it's built for, and the little catches nobody mentions. The live, copyable versions sit on our coupons page whenever you're ready to order.

Every Domino's Deal at a Glance

Before we go one by one, here's the whole landscape in a single view. Bookmark this table and you've basically got the strategy memorized.

DealWhat It DoesBest For
Mix & Match2+ items at a fixed price eachEveryday orders, any size
$6.99 Each3+ items at a low flat priceFamilies, parties, big groups
50% Off Menu PizzasHalf off full-price pizzasA specialty not in the deal
Carryout SpecialDiscount for pickup ordersAnyone who can drive over
Emergency Pizza & wild cardsFree pizza / limited promosRewards members

Mix & Match — The One You'll Use Most

This is the workhorse, the deal you'll come back to again and again. Pick two or more items, pay a fixed price for each, done. Pizzas, sides, pasta, chicken — they nearly all play. What makes it special, and what most people don't realize, is that specialty pizzas usually count too. So you're not stuck ordering a plain cheese just to save money. You can load up a fully dressed specialty and pay the same per-item rate. I broke the whole thing down in the Mix & Match guide, but honestly, this one deal covers the majority of orders you'll ever place.

Who It's Best For

Just about everyone, which is exactly why it's the default. Solo diners pair a pizza with a side. Couples grab two mediums. Families mix a couple of pizzas with bread and a dessert. If you only ever learn one Domino's deal in your life, make it this one.

$6.99 Each When You Buy Three

Feeding a crowd? Bump up to three or more items and each one drops to a low flat price. It quietly beats Mix & Match once you're ordering that much food anyway, so it's always worth comparing the two right there at checkout. Think game night, think a house full of teenagers who somehow eat their weight in pizza, think the office lunch nobody planned properly until 11am. This is the deal that shines the moment the order gets big.

Half Off Menu-Price Pizzas

Every so often Domino's knocks 50% off pizzas ordered at regular menu price. Simple, no gymnastics required, and it's genuinely handy when you want a specialty pie that isn't in this week's Mix & Match rotation. The catch? It's a limited-time thing that comes and goes without much warning. When you spot it in the app, grab it, because it might be gone next week and you'll be kicking yourself.

Carryout Is the Quiet Champion

Want to know the cheapest trick that nobody thinks is a trick? Just go pick it up. Carryout skips the delivery fee entirely — that's four to six bucks back in your pocket before you even factor in a tip — and Domino's regularly runs carryout-only large-pizza specials that undercut everything else on the menu. If your couch can survive a ten-minute round trip, your wallet will genuinely thank you. I lean on this one constantly, and it's the single easiest saving on this whole list.

The Limited-Time Wild Cards

Then there are the headline stunts — things like Emergency Pizza, where rewards members bank a free pie to redeem on a rough day later. These promotions are fun, occasionally very generous, and completely unpredictable. My rule is simple: always check the deals tab in the app before you order, because every so often the wild card beats every standing deal by a mile, and you'd hate to miss it by thirty seconds of impatience. Holidays, big game weekends, and back-to-school season tend to bring the best of these out, so keep an eye out around then.

Which Deal Should You Use? Quick Guide

Deals only help if you pick the right one for your situation. Here's the cheat sheet.

Your SituationReach For
Just you, one dinnerMix & Match (2 items)
Couple or small orderMix & Match
Family or 3+ items$6.99 Each
Want one specialty pizza50% Off Menu, if live
Can pick it upCarryout Special, always

What About Student and Military Discounts?

People ask about these a lot. Domino's discounts here vary widely by location and aren't a guaranteed national thing, so the honest answer is to check with your local store or the app rather than counting on a fixed percentage. Often the standing value deals — Mix & Match and carryout — end up beating a small percentage discount anyway, so don't overlook the everyday deals while hunting for a special one.

How to Enter a Code (and Why Most Apply Themselves)

People ask me where the promo code box lives, and here's the honest answer — you often won't need it at all. Most of Domino's best deals apply automatically the moment you add qualifying items to your cart. When there is a code, it goes in the coupon or deals section at checkout in the app or on the website. If a deal isn't showing up, back out and check that your items actually qualify. Nine times out of ten, that's the entire fix.

Can You Stack Everything? Sort Of.

Let's kill the myth right now: you generally can't slap two coupons on the same pizza. Sorry, that dream isn't real. But you can absolutely layer strategy, which is almost as good. Order through a value deal, choose carryout to kill the delivery fee, and stay logged into Domino's Rewards so every single order quietly builds toward a freebie in the background. Do all three at once and you're saving three different ways without ever needing a magic code. The full math lives in the money-saving guide, and the whole menu with prices is worth a look before you build your cart.

How to Spot a Fake Coupon

One last warning, because it matters. If a code promises something absurd — a totally free large pizza with no purchase, say — it's almost certainly fake or a data-harvesting trap. Real Domino's deals live in the official app and on the official site, full stop. Anything asking you to fill out surveys or hand over personal details to 'unlock' a coupon is a red flag. Stick to official sources and you'll never get burned.

A Quick Reality Check

Deals shift constantly and vary store to store — what's live in one city might not exist two states over. I keep this page current, but we're an independent, unofficial guide, not Domino's HQ. Confirm any offer in the official app before you count on it, and never, ever trust a stranger online promising a guaranteed free-pizza code. If it sounds too good to be true, it almost always is. Order smart, verify at checkout, and enjoy the pizza — that's the whole point.

faqs.question: How many calories are in a slice of Domino's pizza?
faqs.answer: Most Domino's slices land between about 150 and 380 calories. A large Hand Tossed cheese slice is roughly 270 calories, a large pepperoni slice about 300, and a medium Crunchy Thin cheese slice can be as low as 150. Loaded specialty pizzas like the ExtravaganZZa push past 350 per slice.

faqs.question: How many calories are in a whole large Domino's pizza?
faqs.answer: A large 14-inch Hand Tossed cheese pizza is roughly 2,160 calories across its 8 slices, and the pepperoni version is around 2,400. Switching that same large to Crunchy Thin drops it to roughly 1,600 calories.

faqs.question: How many calories are in a medium Domino's pizza?
faqs.answer: A medium 12-inch Hand Tossed cheese pizza is about 1,720 calories in total, or roughly 215 per slice across 8 slices. A medium pepperoni comes in around 1,920 calories.

faqs.question: Which Domino's pizza has the fewest calories?
faqs.answer: A Crunchy Thin cheese or veggie pizza is the lightest thing on the pizza menu — around 150 calories per medium slice. Order it with light cheese and vegetable toppings and you have the lowest-calorie pizza Domino's makes.

faqs.question: Is Domino's thin crust lower in calories?
faqs.answer: Yes, noticeably. Crunchy Thin uses far less dough, so it typically saves 60 to 90 calories per slice compared with Hand Tossed. Over a whole pizza that is often 500 calories or more.

faqs.question: How many calories are in Domino's Stuffed Cheesy Bread?
faqs.answer: Roughly 260 calories for two pieces of the plain version, so a full 8-piece order lands north of 1,000 calories. The Pepperoni and Spinach & Feta versions are slightly higher per piece.

faqs.question: How many calories are in Domino's boneless chicken and wings?
faqs.answer: Boneless chicken is about 50 calories per piece, so an 8-piece order is roughly 400. Plain bone-in wings are around 55 each, and sauced versions such as Hot Buffalo or Sweet BBQ run 65 to 70 per wing before dipping sauce.

faqs.question: Does Domino's show calories when you order?
faqs.answer: Yes. Domino's publishes a nutrition guide and a Cal-O-Meter tool that recalculates calories as you build a pizza, and US stores display calorie information at the point of ordering. That live tool is always more accurate than any third-party chart, including this one.

faqs.question: How many calories are in Domino's Chocolate Lava Crunch Cake?
faqs.answer: About 350 calories per cake. They are sold in twos, so an order is roughly 700 calories if you eat both.

faqs.question: Can you eat Domino's while watching your calories?
faqs.answer: Comfortably, yes — it just takes ordering on purpose. Two slices of medium Crunchy Thin veggie with light cheese is around 300 calories, which fits most days. The calories pile up from the extras: dips, garlic bread, soda and a third or fourth slice.

content:
How Many Calories Are in a Slice of Domino's Pizza?

Short answer first, because that's what you came for: a slice of Domino's pizza runs roughly 150 to 380 calories, depending on size, crust and toppings. A large Hand Tossed cheese slice sits around 270. Add pepperoni and you're near 300. Go Crunchy Thin on a medium and you can drop to about 150 a slice.

That spread is huge — more than double from one end to the other — and it's entirely under your control at checkout. So let me lay out the whole menu, category by category, so you can see exactly where the calories live and where they don't. I'm Dana, I write the nutrition side of this guide, and I'm not here to talk you out of ordering pizza. I'm here to help you order the pizza you actually want without being blindsided by the number.

One honest note before the tables: these are approximate figures for guidance, gathered from published nutrition data. Real numbers move with portioning, toppings and store. When you need precision, build your order in the Domino's app and read the live calorie count — nothing beats that.

Domino's Calories Per Slice by Size

This is the table most people are looking for. Hand Tossed is the default crust, so it's the fair baseline for comparing sizes.

Notice the trap in that table: a large slice isn't a small slice. People assume "two slices" means the same thing everywhere, but two large Hand Tossed pepperoni slices (~600 calories) is nearly the same as three small cheese slices. If you're counting, count the size too, not just the slice. Our Domino's pizza sizes guide breaks down the diameters and how many each one actually feeds.

A word on the newest one: Parmesan Stuffed Crust is Domino's first stuffed crust, and it puts mozzarella inside the rim with Parmesan and garlic seasoning on top. There's no way around it — melted cheese baked into the edge is extra calories on every slice, and it's the one crust I'd genuinely check in the app before ordering rather than estimating. It's a treat crust, and that's fine, as long as you order it knowing that — our Parmesan Stuffed Crust guide covers the price, sizes and whether it's worth the upcharge. The gap between Pacific Veggie and ExtravaganZZa is about 140 calories a slice. Eat three slices and that's a 420-calorie difference from one menu decision. Veggie-forward specialties are the quiet win here — they still taste like a proper loaded pizza, they just don't stack meat on meat on cheese.

It's delicious and I'm not banning it — but it is a main course pretending to be a side, and it should replace a couple of slices rather than sit next to them. Order the same pasta in a dish and you've saved more than a slice of large pepperoni without changing a single thing about the food you actually wanted. Prices for the whole non-pizza range are in our Domino's sides menu guide.

Desserts & Dipping Sauces

Small items, sneaky numbers. Dips especially — nobody logs a dipping cup.

Two lava cakes plus two ranch cups is about 1,040 calories of things you'd probably describe as "just a bit extra." If you love a dip — and I do — marinara is the freebie. It's a fraction of the creamy ones and it goes with everything on the menu.

Don't Forget the Drink

A 20 oz bottle of regular soda is roughly 240 calories, which is very close to an entire extra slice of large cheese pizza. Diet or zero-sugar versions are effectively zero, and bottled water obviously is. Nothing else on this page gives you a ~240-calorie saving for so little sacrifice. Our Domino's drinks guide has the full lineup.

The Lowest-Calorie Domino's Order

Put it all together and here's what a genuinely light order looks like, without pretending you're eating salad:

  • Medium Crunchy Thin, light cheese, veggie toppings — around 130–150 calories a slice
  • Two slices, not four — roughly 300 calories total
  • Marinara instead of ranch — saves ~125 calories a cup
  • A zero-sugar drink — saves ~240 calories
  • Skip the bread bowl, keep the pasta dish — saves ~350–400

That's a real dinner around the 400-calorie mark. Compare it with a casual default order — three large pepperoni slices, half an order of Stuffed Cheesy Bread, ranch and a regular soda — which clears 2,000. Same restaurant, same twenty minutes, five times the calories.

Seven Ways to Cut Calories Without Hating Your Order

None of these require willpower. They're just menu mechanics.

  • Switch to Crunchy Thin. Same price, same toppings, ~500 fewer calories on a large.
  • Ask for light cheese. It's a free modification and it trims 20–30 calories a slice without making the pizza taste bare.
  • Swap one meat for one veg. Pepperoni to peppers is a real cut and the pizza still tastes loaded.
  • Order the size you'll eat, not the size that's cheapest. A large is better value, but only if the extra slices aren't eaten out of proximity.
  • Box the leftovers before you sit down. The fourth slice is almost never hunger.
  • Make the side a starter, not an addition. Wings or cheesy bread, with one fewer slice.
  • Let the drink do the work. Zero-sugar. It's the cheapest 240 calories you'll ever save.

If the goal is trimming the bill as well as the calorie count, the same "order on purpose" logic applies — our money-saving playbook and the current Domino's coupons page cover that side.

How to Check Exact Calories Before You Order

Every number on this page is a guide. Here's how to get the real one for the exact pizza you're about to buy:

  • Build it in the app or on the site. Domino's Cal-O-Meter recalculates as you add and remove toppings, so you see the effect of every choice before you pay.
  • Read the per-slice figure, not the whole-pizza one. Menus often show the pizza total, which looks alarming until you divide by eight.
  • Check the published nutrition guide for sides. Sides and dips vary more between versions than pizzas do.
  • Ask the store about preparation. Useful for allergens especially — the gluten-free crust is prepared in a shared kitchen, so it suits a preference rather than celiac disease.

How to Read These Numbers

I'd rather be straight with you than look authoritative. Third-party calorie charts for Domino's disagree with each other, sometimes by 30 or 40 calories a slice, because portioning is done by hand, toppings vary, sizes get cut differently and recipes get updated. The figures here are rounded, cross-checked against published nutrition data, and meant for planning, not tracking to the gram.

What doesn't change is the shape of the data, and that's the genuinely useful part: thin beats thick, veggie beats meat, dish beats bread bowl, marinara beats ranch, and the drink matters more than you'd think. Get those five right and the exact number stops being something you need to worry about. content:
What Mix & Match Really Is

Think of Mix & Match as Domino's leaning over the counter and saying, pick a few things, we'll charge you a flat rate for each, stop overthinking it. That's basically the whole pitch. You choose two or more qualifying items, and every one lands at the same fixed price. No coupon to remember, no code to fumble at checkout, no fine print to squint at under your phone light. It just works, and that simplicity is half the reason it's outlasted nearly every other deal Domino's has ever run.

What I love about it — and I order a genuinely embarrassing amount of pizza, so trust me here — is the flexibility. You're not forced to buy two of the same thing the way some deals sneakily require. Grab a pizza and a side. Grab three totally different items. Get a pizza for you and pasta for your partner who's suddenly 'not in a pizza mood' tonight. The deal honestly doesn't care what you mix, and that freedom is exactly why it beats the fussier, more rigid promos out there.

Now, the exact per-item price moves around a bit over time and from store to store, because every Domino's is franchised and priced on its own. For years it's hovered in the same rough neighborhood, and the app always shows you the live number before you pay. Treat any figure in this guide as a realistic example, then let checkout confirm the real total. Deal? Good. Let's get into the useful stuff.

What Actually Qualifies

The eligible list is refreshingly generous, which is the best part of the whole thing. Medium two-topping pizzas, Stuffed Cheesy Bread, bread twists, oven-baked pasta, boneless chicken, and quite often salads and desserts too. But here's the kicker most people walk straight past: the medium specialty pizzas usually count. So a fully loaded ExtravaganZZa can cost you the same per-item price as a plain cheese. Read that twice. Why on earth would you order plain, then? Load it up. That's free flavor sitting right there on the table.

Here's a quick map of what typically plays and what doesn't, so you can build a cart in your head before you even open the app.

CategoryUsually Qualifies?Notes
Medium 2-topping pizzaYesThe classic building block of the deal
Medium specialty pizzaYesA few premium pies may add a small upcharge
Stuffed Cheesy Bread & bread twistsYesGreat low-cost filler for the table
Oven-baked pastaYesPerfect for the non-pizza eater
Boneless chicken & wingsUsuallyAdds protein without breaking the deal
Desserts & saladsOftenVaries by store and current promo
Large or XL pizzasNoMix & Match is built around the medium
DrinksSometimesCheck the app; a 2-liter is cheap regardless

The One Small Catch

A handful of premium or ultra-loaded specialty pizzas may carry a tiny upcharge, and some stores quietly tweak what's eligible. It's not a big deal, and you'll never get ambushed by it, because the app tells you exactly what qualifies as you build the order. The running total updates live with every item you add. So there's no guessing and no ugly surprise at the end. Watch that number climb, and you'll always know precisely where you stand before you commit.

Ordering for One (Yes, It Still Works)

People assume Mix & Match is a family-only deal. It isn't, and that myth costs solo diners money. Eating alone doesn't lock you out even slightly. Pair a medium two-topping with an order of boneless chicken or some cheesy bread, and you've got a proper dinner tonight plus a guaranteed lunch tomorrow. Since the price is fixed per item, leaning toward a specialty pizza just gets you more going on for the exact same cash. And honestly? Cold leftover specialty pizza at noon the next day is one of life's genuinely small, reliable joys. Don't let anyone tell you otherwise.

A Sample Solo Cart

Picture this order: one medium specialty pizza, one order of boneless chicken. Two items, both at the deal rate, and you're eating twice off it. That's a dinner and a lunch for the price most places charge for a single sad combo meal. Add a 20 oz drink if you want to round it out.

Ordering for the Whole Table

Feeding a family? This is where the deal really earns its keep and stops being clever and starts being essential. Two medium pizzas — say one pepperoni and one plain cheese for the picky kid who refuses anything with 'bits' on it — plus a shareable side and a dessert covers every mouth at the table without drama. I laid out several ready-to-tap combos in the family picks guide so you don't have to reinvent the wheel every Friday night. Toss in a 2-liter and nobody's asking for anything else for the rest of the evening.

The Three-Pizza Sweet Spot

Once you're ordering for four or more, three or four items becomes the natural size, and that's exactly when you should compare Mix & Match against the $6.99 Each deal, which I'll break down in a second. Bigger orders unlock better per-item math, so a full family order is genuinely one of the cheapest ways to eat per person at Domino's.

Mix & Match or $6.99 Each? Let's Settle It

Good question, and the honest answer depends entirely on how hungry your group is. Both are per-item deals, but they trigger at different thresholds, and knowing which to reach for saves real money.

DealMinimum ItemsBest ForWatch Out For

$6.99 Each3 or moreFamilies, parties, group ordersNeeds three items to trigger
50% Off Menu PizzasMenu-price pizzasA single specialty not in the dealLimited-time, comes and goes

My rule is dead simple. Build the cart, then glance at both totals right there at checkout and take whichever's lower. It takes thirty seconds and it routinely shaves a few bucks off. For a full rundown of every current offer, our coupons page keeps the live list.

Which Items Give You the Most Value?

Let's be strategic, because not every qualifying item is equal value inside the deal. Since the price per item is fixed, you want to fill your slots with the things that would normally cost the most on their own. That means specialty pizzas over plain ones, and Stuffed Cheesy Bread over a basic bread twist. The pepperoni is a safe crowd-pleaser, but if the deal lets you swap to a loaded specialty for the same money, take it every time. You're essentially getting the premium toppings thrown in for nothing.

How to Actually Order It, Step by Step

There's no secret handshake here, which is part of the charm. Open the Domino's app or website, head to the deals or Mix & Match section, and start adding qualifying items to your cart. The deal price applies automatically as you hit the item minimum — no code to paste, no hoops. If it isn't showing up, back out and double-check your items actually qualify, because that's almost always the reason. Pick carryout if you can, and make sure you're signed into your rewards account before you pay.

Getting the Rock-Bottom Total

Want the absolute cheapest version of any Mix & Match order? Stack three habits and don't skip any of them. Order through Mix & Match, choose carryout to dodge the delivery fee entirely, and stay signed into Domino's Rewards so the order still quietly banks points toward a free pizza down the line. That's a deal, a saved fee, and future free food all bundled into one order. Do that consistently and the savings pile up faster than you'd expect over a month or two. My complete method lives in the money-saving playbook if you want the whole system.

The Mistakes People Make

Two big ones, and I see them constantly. First, ordering plain items when a specialty qualifies for the same price — that's just leaving flavor on the counter for no reason. Second, defaulting to delivery out of habit when carryout would've saved the fee entirely. Neither mistake is dramatic on its own, but together they quietly inflate order after order. Now that you know, you won't make them.

The Bottom Line

Mix & Match is the deal I'd teach a total Domino's newcomer first, before anything else. It's flexible, it's simple, it covers solo dinners and family feasts alike, and it stacks beautifully with carryout and rewards. The exact per-item price shifts now and then and varies store to store, so let the checkout screen have the final word every time. We're an independent, unofficial guide here — Domino's writes the real rules. But of all the rules they've written, this deal is easily the best one.

Domino's is already decent value on its own. But most folks walk right past the savings without noticing, ordering at full menu price like it's the only option on the table. It isn't. Not even close. So build your entire order inside one of them from the very first click, not as an afterthought at the end. Ordering full-price and hoping to fix it later is exactly how people end up paying twenty percent too much without ever realizing it happened.

2. Go Get It Yourself

Delivery tacks on a fee, usually four to six bucks, before you've even thought about a tip. That's real money on a small order — sometimes a third of the whole bill. If picking up is even remotely convenient, carryout wins, full stop. The short version fits on a bumper sticker: your car is cheaper than their driver. And carryout-only specials, which you'll find on the coupons page, often sweeten the deal even further beyond just skipping the fee.

3. Order Through the App

Phone orders quietly miss the best pricing, and a surprising number of people still don't know this. The app and website reflect the current national promotions and unlock carryout-only specials you literally cannot get by calling the store. It's a couple of taps for a genuine discount. If you're still dialing the number out of habit, you're leaving money on the counter every single time.

4. Join Rewards — It's Free

Every qualifying order quietly banks points toward a free pizza, and signing up costs you absolutely nothing. There's no annual fee, no catch, no reason on earth not to. Over a few months of normal ordering, that's a free pie you'd otherwise have paid full price for. The full breakdown's in the rewards explainer, but the summary is simple — be signed in every time so no order goes uncounted.

5. Size Up on Purpose

Here's a bit of pizza economics people consistently miss. The gap between a medium and a large is often just a dollar or two, but you get a lot more pizza for that dollar. Measured per slice, the large is usually the smartest buy on the whole board, and the sizes guide proves it with the numbers. Don't be shy about sizing up, especially when you're feeding more than one person — the leftovers alone justify it.

Since specialty pizzas usually qualify for Mix & Match at the same per-item price as a basic pie, ordering one is basically getting a pile of premium toppings for free. There's genuinely no downside here.

7. Cut the Stuff You Won't Finish

Extra dips, premium toppings, that second dessert nobody actually asked for — it all quietly creeps onto the total while you're not looking. The app is very, very good at nudging you toward add-ons. Order what you'll genuinely eat, not what looks tempting on the screen at 9pm when everything sounds like a great idea. Be a little ruthless in the cart and you'll thank yourself at checkout.

8. Watch for the Wild Cards

Limited-time promos like Emergency Pizza or a 50%-off-menu week can occasionally beat the standing deals by a wide margin. Peek at the deals tab before you commit — it takes five seconds and every so often it saves you ten dollars flat. The wild cards are unpredictable, which is exactly why checking becomes a reflex worth building into every order.

9. Split a Big Order

The $6.99 Each deal rewards bulk, so pooling an order with roommates, coworkers or family absolutely crushes the per-person cost. Everyone throws in a few bucks, you hit the three-item threshold easily, and suddenly dinner costs everyone less than a sad fast-food combo. Pizza's always been cheaper by the crowd — that's kind of its whole thing, and it's a lever most people forget they have.

Stack It All Together

content:
Is It Even Worth It? Short Answer: Yeah.

Loyalty programs can be a real hassle — endless tiers, points that vanish the moment you forget about them, apps that nag you every other day with notifications you didn't ask for. So I completely understand the skepticism. But Domino's Rewards, the one half of us still call Piece of the Pie out of pure habit, is refreshingly simple by comparison. You order, you earn, you eventually get free food. That's the entire loop, start to finish. If you buy Domino's even once a month, joining is a genuine no-brainer, because it costs you nothing and quietly discounts a future order while you're not even paying attention.

This guide walks through exactly how it works, what you earn, what you can cash in for, whether it's actually worth your time, and the small habits that squeeze the most out of it. No fluff. Let's get into it.

How to Sign Up (It Takes Two Minutes)

There's almost nothing to it, which is the point. Create a free account in the Domino's app or on the website, and you're enrolled in rewards from your very next qualifying order. No membership fee, no card to carry, no commitment. If you already order Domino's without an account, you've literally been leaving free pizza on the table this whole time. Fix that today and your future self will thank you in about six orders.

How the Points Add Up

The classic setup hands you 10 points for every qualifying order of five dollars or more, calculated before tax and tip. And here's a detail people really appreciate — it doesn't matter one bit whether you're getting delivery or carryout. Points are points either way. Domino's has also tested newer tiered versions that let you cash in smaller point totals for smaller items, so the genuinely smart move is to glance at the current catalogue in the app before you assume the old rules still apply. These programs evolve, and this one has changed shape more than once over the years.

Qualifying order of $5+ (before tax/tip)10 points
Delivery or carryoutSame points either way
Ordering through a deal like Mix & MatchStill earns full points
Signing up / occasional bonus promosExtra points, varies

Do Points Expire?

They can, and this trips a lot of people up. Points generally lapse after a stretch of account inactivity, so if you order Domino's a few times a year you're perfectly fine, but if you go completely dormant for ages, don't be shocked to find your balance reset to zero one day. The fix couldn't be simpler — just placing a qualifying order keeps the whole thing alive and ticking. Use it or slowly lose it, basically. It's not aggressive about it, but it's worth knowing.

The Free Pizza Math

Let's talk about the payoff, because that's really why you're here. Under the traditional program, 60 points gets you a free medium two-topping pizza. That's roughly six qualifying orders — not instant gratification, sure, but honestly not a marathon either. Order weekly and you're eating free within about a month and a half. Some of the newer options let you trade as few as 20 points for a side or a dessert, which is a genuinely nice touch when you don't feel like holding out for the full pie. Want a lava cake right now instead of a pizza in six weeks? That flexibility is welcome.

Is It Actually Worth It? Let's Do Real Numbers

Here's the honest math. If a free medium two-topping is worth roughly ten bucks and it takes about six qualifying orders to earn, you're effectively getting a small discount baked into every single order without lifting a finger. Compare that to the loyalty programs at some other chains, which pile on confusing tiers and expiration traps, and Domino's simplicity starts to look like a feature rather than a limitation. It won't make you rich. But free pizza every couple of months for doing something you were already going to do? That's a quiet, easy win.

Getting the Most Out of It

Here's a thing worth knowing that saves you from a pointless mistake. Points come per order, not per dollar spent. So splitting one giant order into a bunch of tiny ones to farm extra points is way more hassle than it's worth, and frankly a little silly. Don't bother. The only habit that actually matters is making sure you're signed in every single time, so no order ever slips through uncounted. That's genuinely it. Then pair rewards with a value deal and carryout, and now you're stacking savings on top of savings on top of a slow drip toward free food.

The One Habit That Matters Most

Log in before you order. Every time. That's the whole trick. People lose out not because the program is stingy but because they check out as a guest and forget. Make signing in the first thing you do, and the points take care of themselves.

Rewards and Deals Play Nice Together

This is the part that quietly makes the whole thing worth it. You still earn points when you order through Mix & Match or a carryout special — the deal discount and the points aren't mutually exclusive, which surprises people. So over a few months of totally normal ordering, you're pocketing a free pizza on top of the discounts you were already getting anyway. It's not flashy. There's no confetti when it happens. It just works, steadily, in the background, and one day you open the app and realize there's a free pie sitting there waiting for you. The whole cost-cutting picture fits together in the money-saving guide, and it pairs perfectly with the offers on our coupons page.

The Fine Print, Because There's Always Fine Print

Point values, redemption tiers and qualifying minimums are all set by Domino's, and they shift from time to time without much fanfare or warning. We're an independent, unofficial guide, so before you go counting on a specific reward at checkout, double-check the current terms in the official app. Nobody likes getting to that final screen expecting a free pizza that quietly isn't there anymore. Verify first, then enjoy the win. And if you order Domino's with any regularity at all, that win is coming sooner than you think.

Twelve inches, eight slices. Enough for one genuinely hungry person, or two people who are treating pizza as a snack rather than the main event. But here's the fact worth tucking away: the medium two-topping is the classic Mix & Match building block, which is precisely why this size shows up in so many deals. If you're ordering to a promotion, medium is often the size that unlocks the best pricing. When in doubt, medium plays nicely with just about every offer Domino's runs.

Large — 14 Inches (The One I'd Order)

Fourteen inches, eight slices, and almost always the best bang for your buck on the entire menu. I'll be blunt — this is the size I default to nine times out of ten. The price bump from medium to large is usually just a couple of dollars, but you get noticeably more pizza for it. Here's why: a pizza's area grows with the square of its radius, so a 14-inch large actually holds a lot more pizza than a 12-inch medium, not just a little more. Do the per-slice math and the large quietly wins nearly every time. Feeding two or more people? Start here and stop overthinking it.

The Per-Slice Value Truth

People obsess over the sticker price and miss the real question, which is cost per slice, or better yet, cost per square inch of actual pizza. When you measure it that way, the medium-to-large jump is one of the best value moves in fast food. You're paying a small premium for a big chunk more food. A large pepperoni through a deal is, pound for pound, hard to beat.

Extra Large — 16 Inches

This one's a bit of a specialist, and I mean that as a compliment. Sixteen inches, available on Brooklyn Style crust only, cut into six big, thin, foldable New-York-style slices. It's the most pizza Domino's will hand you in a single pie, and those foldable slices are honestly just fun to eat — there's something deeply satisfying about folding a slice in half, street-vendor style. If you're chasing that classic pizzeria vibe rather than maximum topping thickness, the Extra Large is your pick. Just remember it's Brooklyn crust only, so if you're a deep-dish-at-heart person, this isn't your lane.

How Many Pizzas Do You Actually Need?

This is the question that really matters when you're ordering for a group, and guessing wrong means either hungry guests or a fridge full of sad leftovers. Here's my rough planning table. It assumes normal appetites, so bump it up for teenagers or a football crowd.

PeopleSuggested OrderWhy
11 Small or MediumA full meal with little or no waste
21 LargeBest value, likely a slice or two left over
3–42 LargeBeats one XL on both quantity and price
5–63 Large (use $6.99 Each)Bulk deals kick in and crush the per-person cost
7+4+ Large or a party orderSee the family and catering approach

So Which One Do You Actually Order?

Let me make this dead simple. Eating solo? A small or medium is plenty — lean small if you truly don't want leftovers. Just the two of you? Large, easy call, don't second-guess it. Three or more mouths at the table? Here's the move most people get wrong: skip the single Extra Large and grab two larges through a value deal instead. You'll come out ahead on both total quantity and price, and everyone gets more topping choice. For a full family game plan, the family picks guide maps it all out combo by combo.

Don't Forget the Crust

Size is only half the decision — crust matters just as much, sometimes more. Hand Tossed is the pillowy default, Handmade Pan the indulgent one, Crunchy Thin for the anti-bread crowd, and Brooklyn Style for those big foldable slices. Not every crust comes in every size, either. You'll find the full crust and size pairings on the menu and prices page before you lock in your order.

A Trick for Kids and Parties

Slice counts are standard out of the oven, but you're not stuck with them. You can ask the store to cut a large into ten or twelve smaller pieces at no extra charge, which is a genuine lifesaver at kids' parties where tiny hands and giant slices don't mix. Little request, big difference when there's a crowd of small humans involved.

A Quick Word on Calories

Bigger pizza, more calories — no surprise there. But the slice size matters as much as the count. A large slice packs more than a small one, so 'just one slice' isn't the same across sizes. If you're watching intake, ordering a smaller size and pairing it with a zero-sugar drink is an easy lever, as is choosing Crunchy Thin crust, which trims some of the dough. For the exact per-slice numbers by size and crust, see our Domino's calories and nutrition guide.

One Last Thing

Prices bounce around by location — a large in a big city might run a couple dollars more than the same pie in a small town, and that's just how franchising works. Since this is an independent, unofficial guide, the official Domino's app always has the final say on what you'll actually pay. Use this to plan the right size and the right number of pizzas, then let checkout confirm the number. Order smart, and nobody leaves the table hungry or overcharged. That's the whole goal.

content:
Ordering for a Family Is Basically Diplomacy

Anyone who's fed a table of kids and grown-ups at once knows the drill. One won't touch a vegetable. One wants everything on it, extra everything. Someone's suddenly decided this week that they don't like cheese, which, at a pizza dinner, is a genuinely bold stance to take. The trick isn't hunting for one magical pizza that pleases everybody — that pizza doesn't exist and never has. The real trick is covering all the bases without blowing the budget or losing your mind. Try the interactive picks at the top of the page for ready-to-tap combos, then stick around for the reasoning, the bundles, and a few tricks for the tricky eaters. Prices here are examples, so double-check at checkout as always.

The Safe Bets for Kids

Start with the reliable stuff. A classic pepperoni or a plain cheese on Hand Tossed crust is your foundation, full stop. These are the pizzas that vanish without a single complaint, and ordered through a value deal they barely dent the total. Don't underestimate boring, either — boring feeds children reliably, night after night, and on a chaotic weeknight that reliability is worth its weight in gold. Got a really picky one? Ask for light cheese or just a light sprinkle of pepperoni so it still feels like 'their' pizza with zero surprises to negotiate over.

Something for the Grown-Ups

Now give the adults something with a little ambition, because they deserve a real dinner too, not just the crusts the kids abandoned. A Large pepperoni sitting next to the fully loaded ExtravaganZZa covers both the plain crowd and the folks who actually want some flavor happening on their slice. And if your household skips pork for any reason, the Philly Cheese Steak is a genuinely great shout — no pork, all savory, and it feels a bit special without costing a cent extra inside a deal. Mixing one 'safe' pizza with one 'interesting' pizza is the single most reliable family formula I know, and I've tested it more times than I can count.

Handling Allergies and Dietary Needs

Every family has its constraints, and pizza night shouldn't leave anyone out. If someone's vegetarian, the Pacific Veggie is a proper pizza in its own right, not a sad afterthought. Avoiding pork? The Philly Cheese Steak and plenty of chicken options have you covered. Gluten a concern? There's a Small Gluten Free crust, though it's made in a shared kitchen, so it suits a preference more than a serious medical allergy. The point is, you can almost always build an order where every single person at the table has something they're genuinely happy to eat. That's the goal.

Sides Do the Heavy Lifting

Here's where a lot of family orders quietly fall short — they stop at pizza. Don't. Stuffed Cheesy Bread and boneless chicken stretch the meal further and, crucially, give the kid who's 'not in a pizza mood' an actual escape hatch. There's always one, every single time. And a 2-liter is by far the cheapest way to keep everyone's cup full without buying six separate bottles that cost more and create a pile of trash. Little decisions, but they add up to a smoother, cheaper, less argumentative dinner.

Ready-Made Family Bundles

You don't have to build this from scratch every time. Here are the go-to bundles I reach for, sized by crowd. Adjust for appetites — a table of teenagers eats like a table of adults and then some.

CrowdThe OrderRough Deal Route
Family of 32 medium pizzas + cheesy breadMix & Match
Family of 42 large pizzas + 1 side + 2-literMix & Match, carryout
Family of 5–63 pizzas + boneless chicken + dessert$6.99 Each
Birthday / party4+ pizzas + multiple sides + drinks$6.99 Each or party order

The Cheat-Sheet Rule of Thumb

Let me hand you the formula I actually lean on so you never have to guess again. Two large pizzas, one shareable side, one 2-liter comfortably feeds a family of four with leftovers waiting for tomorrow's lunch. That's your baseline, memorize it. Order the whole thing through Mix & Match and grab it carryout, and you've fed the entire crew for a very reasonable number — the kind that doesn't make you wince when you tap pay. Bigger family? Add a third pizza and lean on the $6.99 Each deal instead. The interactive picks tool up top gives you a few tuned-up versions depending on the size and mood of your crew.

Feeding a Birthday Party or Big Group

When the crowd gets past six, the rules shift a little. Order more variety, not just more of the same, because a room full of kids will have wildly different opinions and you want easy wins. A stack of pepperoni and cheese covers the safe crowd, one or two specialties keep the adults happy, and a couple of shareable sides fill the gaps. Lean hard on the $6.99 Each deal here — it's built for exactly this kind of bulk order, and it keeps the per-head cost genuinely low. Order ahead of time if you can, especially on a busy weekend evening, so a big order doesn't leave you waiting while hungry kids stage a small revolt.

Squeezing the Price Down

The money-saving rules are the same as always, they just matter far more when you're buying for a whole table. Choose carryout to kill the delivery fee, order in the app to catch the best pricing and browse the current deals, and stay logged into Domino's Rewards so even the big family order banks points toward a free pizza down the line. Family orders are large, which means they earn and save more than a solo order ever could — so use that scale to your advantage instead of letting it work against you. The full method's laid out in the money-saving playbook.

The Bottom Line

Feeding a family at Domino's isn't about finding one perfect pizza. It's about mixing safe and interesting, propping the meal up with a couple of smart sides, and running the whole thing through a deal so the total stays friendly. Do that, and you get the rare weeknight miracle: a table where everyone's actually eating and nobody's complaining. We're an independent, unofficial guide, so let the official app confirm the real prices and deals before you pay. Then go enjoy the quiet, and maybe grab a slice for yourself before it's gone.

content:
Why Everyone Searches This

Domino's basically built its entire reputation on delivery — fast, trackable, dependable, the pizza that actually shows up when it says it will. So when the craving hits at 8pm and you type 'Domino's delivery near me' into your phone, you're in very good company. Millions of people do the exact same thing every single day. Let's cut through the noise and cover what actually matters: finding the right store, knowing how long you'll really wait, understanding that fee, tipping the right way, tracking your order, and spending as little as humanly possible getting a hot pizza to your front door. Everything you need, in one place.

First, Find Your Store

Delivery gets handled by whichever franchise store covers your specific address, so step one is confirming you're actually inside a delivery zone. Use the official locator, or start from our store locator to zero in on your city and get pointed the right way. And here's an honest heads-up nobody likes to hear — not every address makes the cut. If you live way out in the countryside or on the far edge of a coverage map, you might be carryout-only. It's not personal, it's just how the delivery zones fall, and it's far better to know that before you've got your heart set on a doorstep pizza that isn't coming.

How Long You'll Actually Wait

Most delivery orders land somewhere in that 25-to-40-minute window, which is honestly pretty solid for hot food to your door. But let's be real about when it stretches, because managing your expectations saves a lot of frustration.

When You OrderTypical WaitWhy
Weekday, off-peak20–30 minStores are quiet, drivers are free
Friday / Saturday dinner rush35–50 minEveryone orders at once
Big game or holiday45–60+ minPeak demand, limited drivers
Bad weatherAdd 10–20 minSlower, more careful driving

The app's live tracker walks you through every stage, from the dough being prepped to your driver pulling out of the lot, so you're never left standing by the window guessing. If timing is tight — say you've got hungry kids or people arriving — ordering a little earlier than you think you need to is always the smart move.

The Fee Nobody Loves (and How It Breaks Down)

Expect a delivery fee somewhere in the four-to-six-dollar range, set by your local store. And this next part is important, so I'm going to say it as plainly as I possibly can: that fee is not a tip. Your driver does not pocket it. It goes to the store to cover the cost of running delivery. So if you can swing it, tip your driver separately — they're the actual reason your dinner arrived warm instead of lukewarm, and they're very often driving their own car and paying for their own gas to do it.

ChargeRoughlyWho Gets It
Delivery fee$3.99–$5.99The store, not the driver
Tip (recommended)15–20% or a few dollarsYour driver
Small-order surchargeVariesThe store, if below the minimum

How Much Should You Tip?

A fair rule is 15 to 20 percent of the order, or a few dollars minimum on a smaller one, and bump it up in rotten weather or for a long drive. Drivers work hard for reasonable pay, and a decent tip genuinely matters to them. It's the part of the bill I'd cut last, not first.

Tracking It Down to the Minute

Give Domino's credit here — the Tracker is genuinely one of the better ordering tools any chain has ever built. It shows your pizza moving through prep, into the oven, past the quality check, and finally out the door with a named driver, all updating in real time. It's oddly satisfying to watch, honestly, and it takes the anxiety out of the wait. The stages are simple: your order is prepped, then baked, then given a quick quality check, then handed to a driver for delivery. When you see that last stage flip, it's time to make sure someone's near the door. A quick tip — double-check your address and any gate codes before you submit, since a wrong detail is the number-one reason a smooth order suddenly goes sideways.

Delivery vs Carryout: The Honest Comparison

Real talk, because I'd rather be honest than flattering — delivery will always cost more than carryout once that fee and a fair tip stack up. There's simply no way around it. Here's the trade-off laid bare.

FactorDeliveryCarryout
Extra feesDelivery fee + tipNone
Exclusive dealsFewerCarryout-only specials
ConvenienceHighest — you don't moveA short trip
Best forBad weather, no car, pure comfortSaving money

If you can possibly pick it up yourself, a carryout deal beats delivery every single time, no contest.

How to Spend Less on Delivery

Sometimes you're just set on delivery, and that's completely fair — that's kind of the whole appeal. When you go that route, do this to soften the cost: order through Mix & Match to lock in low per-item pricing, hit any delivery minimum efficiently rather than padding your cart with junk you won't eat, and stay signed into Domino's Rewards so the order still earns toward a free pizza later. Choosing a large over a medium also stretches your money further per slice. You'll never make delivery cheaper than carryout, but you can absolutely make it hurt a lot less. The complete system is in the money-saving guide.

Late-Night Cravings, Covered

Here's one of Domino's genuinely underrated strengths. A lot of stores deliver late — frequently till midnight, sometimes all the way to one in the morning — which makes it the reliable go-to when basically nothing else is open and you're wide awake and hungry. We've all been there at least once. Just confirm your specific store's hours on the hours page or directly in the app, because closing times swing quite a bit by location, and you don't want to place a mental order for a store that shut twenty minutes ago.

Common Delivery Problems (and Quick Fixes)

Even a great system hiccups now and then. If your pizza shows up cold, it's usually a long drive or a delay on your end getting to the door — the tracker helps you catch it coming. If something's wrong or missing from the order, the app and the store can sort it out, so hang onto your order confirmation. And if the driver can't find you, a clear address, a unit number, and a quick note about the buzzer or gate solves it before it starts. Little bits of prep on your side keep the whole thing smooth.

Order With Confidence

Delivery availability, timing, and fees are all set by individual franchises and shift constantly with demand, so let the checkout screen confirm the real details before you commit. This is an independent, unofficial guide, written purely to help you order smarter and spend less — not to take your order or quote you a guaranteed price. And when you're ready to plan the actual food, swing by our Domino's menu with prices guide for the full rundown of what everything costs. Now go get that pizza. You've earned it.

content:
Domino's Finally Made a Stuffed Crust

For years there was one obvious question in the Domino's app that had a disappointing answer: where's the stuffed crust? Pizza Hut had owned that idea since the nineties, and Domino's simply didn't have one. That changed in March 2025, when Domino's launched Parmesan Stuffed Crust — the first stuffed crust in the company's history, and a permanent menu item rather than a limited-time test.

So it's real, it's not going anywhere, and the question now is a practical one: what does it cost, which size can you get it in, how many calories does it add, and is it actually worth the upcharge over the crust you already order? Let's go through all of it properly. And the usual honest note first — every price here is an example, because Domino's stores are individually franchised and price independently. The checkout screen is the only number that counts.

What's Actually Inside the Crust

The name is slightly misleading, so let's clear it up straight away. The cheese stuffed inside the rim is mozzarella — 100% real mozzarella, baked into a buttery-flavoured dough. The Parmesan is on the outside: the crust is finished with Domino's garlic seasoning and a sprinkle of Parmesan across the top of the rim.

That's a meaningful difference from what most people picture. This isn't a Parmesan-filled crust; it's a mozzarella-filled crust wearing a garlic-Parmesan coat. And that outer seasoning is genuinely what makes it taste different from every other crust on the menu — you get savoury, garlicky, slightly salty edges rather than the plain bread rim you'd normally leave on the plate.

Domino's Stuffed Crust Price

Here's roughly what to expect. Remember these move by location.

OrderSizeExample Price
Cheese, Parmesan Stuffed CrustMedium 12"~$10.99
One topping, Parmesan Stuffed CrustMedium 12"~$10.99–$12.99
Mix & Match, 2-topping, 2+ pizzasMedium 12"~$10.99 each
Same pizza on Hand TossedMedium 12"~$9.99–$10.99

The number that actually matters is the gap, and the stuffed crust upcharge typically lands between about $1 and $3 per pizza. On one pizza that's nothing — it's less than a dipping cup. On a family order of four pizzas it's a real $8 to $12, which is worth thinking about before you tap it on every pie out of habit. Our money-saving playbook covers where else that money leaks.

Which Sizes Can You Get It In?

This is the most common point of confusion, so let me be precise about what's known and what varies.

Parmesan Stuffed Crust launched on the medium 12-inch, and medium remains the core size at most stores. Promotions have periodically opened it up more widely — Domino's added it to a $9.99 "any crust, any toppings" offer, for example — but that isn't the same as it being permanently available in every size everywhere.

The reliable test takes ten seconds: open the app, choose your size first, then look at the crust list. If Parmesan Stuffed Crust greys out when you switch to large, your store doesn't offer it in that size. That beats any chart on the internet, including this one. If you're weighing sizes generally, our pizza sizes and prices guide breaks down what each one actually feeds.

Calories: The Honest Number

Cheese baked into the rim isn't free, and this is where stuffed crust asks the most of you.

Medium 12" pizzaPer SliceWhole Pizza

Parmesan Stuffed Crust, pepperoni~330 cal~2,640 cal

Crunchy Thin, cheese~150 cal~1,200 cal

So you're paying roughly 100 extra calories per slice versus Hand Tossed — around 800 across a medium pizza. A medium stuffed crust pizza carries more total calories than a large Hand Tossed cheese pizza does. That's not a reason to avoid it; it's a reason to treat it as the indulgent order it is, rather than your default. Full numbers for every crust and size are in our Domino's calories and nutrition guide.

How It Stacks Up Against the Other Crusts

Domino's now has six crusts, and stuffed crust sits at one clear end of the range.

CrustTextureSizesBest For
Crunchy ThinCrisp, cracker-likeS / M / LLightest option
Hand TossedSoft, chewyS / M / LThe everyday default

Handmade PanThick, butteryS / MRich and indulgent
Gluten FreeFirm, compactS onlyAvoiding wheat
Parmesan StuffedFilled, seasoned rimM (check store)Making the crust the point

The honest framing is that Parmesan Stuffed Crust and Handmade Pan compete for the same job — the treat pizza. Pan gives you a thick, buttery base; stuffed crust gives you a filled, seasoned edge. If you're the person who eats the crust first, stuffed wins. If you want richness throughout the whole slice, Pan is your pizza. Our crust types guide covers all six in detail.

Domino's vs Pizza Hut Stuffed Crust

You can't write about this without addressing the comparison everyone makes, so here it is fairly.

Pizza Hut has had stuffed crust for decades and it's the benchmark — a simple cheese-filled rim that delivers a clean cheese pull. Domino's took a different angle, layering garlic seasoning and Parmesan across the top of the rim, so the edge tastes seasoned and savoury rather than purely cheesy.

Neither is objectively better; they're aiming at different cravings. If what you want is the pure nostalgic cheese pull, Pizza Hut still owns that. If you like garlic-butter breadstick flavour and want your crust to actually taste of something, the Domino's version is the more interesting one. Where Domino's usually has the advantage is on the surrounding order — the deals and coupons and the rewards programme tend to make the total cheaper.

Which Toppings Work Best on It

Stuffed crust changes the balance of the pizza, so a couple of pairings work noticeably better than others:

  • Pepperoni — the classic, and the salt plays well with the garlic-Parmesan edge
  • Plain cheese — lets the crust be the whole point, which is arguably why you ordered it
  • Italian sausage and peppers — savoury enough to keep up with a seasoned rim
  • Anything sweet, like pineapple — genuinely divisive here; the garlic seasoning fights the sweetness
  • Heavily loaded meat combinations — the pizza gets very rich very fast when the crust is already filled

One practical tip: because the rim is doing so much work, ordering fewer toppings than usual is not a downgrade on this crust. A one-topping stuffed crust often eats better than a four-topping one, and it keeps you inside the cheaper deal tiers.

How to Order It (and the Deals to Watch)

It's a crust option, not a separate menu item, which trips people up when they go hunting for it under specialty pizzas.

  • Start a build-your-own pizza in the app or on the website, not a specialty recipe
  • Pick your size first — medium is the safest bet for availability
  • Choose Parmesan Stuffed Crust from the crust list, then add toppings
  • Check the deals tab before you pay — the same pizza is often cheaper inside an active offer

On deals specifically: Domino's has run Parmesan Stuffed Crust inside its $9.99 Best Deal Ever promotion at no extra charge, and it regularly appears in Mix & Match style pricing at around $10.99 each on two-topping pizzas. Those offers rotate and expire, so treat the current coupons page as the source of truth, and read our Mix & Match explainer if you want to understand how the multi-pizza pricing actually works. Carryout is worth a look too — the carryout deals guide covers where pickup beats delivery pricing.

So Is It Worth It?

Here's the straight verdict, split by who's asking.

Order it if you're buying one or two pizzas as a treat, you actually eat the crust rather than leaving a graveyard of rims in the box, or you've been ordering elsewhere purely because Domino's didn't have a stuffed crust. A dollar or two for a filled, seasoned edge is decent value, and it turns the least interesting part of the pizza into the best part.

Skip it if you're feeding a crowd and the upcharge multiplies across four or five pizzas, you're watching calories closely, or you're the sort who leaves the crust anyway — in which case you'd be paying extra for the bit you don't eat. In those cases Hand Tossed remains the smarter buy, and Crunchy Thin the lighter one.

What's not in doubt is that it fills a real gap. Domino's went years without an answer to the most-requested crust in the category, and now there's one worth ordering on purpose.
